quiz-warmup.script: Let's start with a simple question about a camera. When an object gets closer, its bounding box usually looks taller in the frame, right? So here's the puzzle: could we draw a single straight line that turns box height into a distance estimate? The answer is yes, in principle — we gather examples of box heights paired with real distances, fit the best line through them, and use it to predict for a brand new box we've never seen. That's exactly what regression is, and today we'll test whether a straight line is truly the right shape for this job.

story-galton.script: Here's a fun bit of history for you. Back in the 1880s, a scientist named Francis Galton measured hundreds of parents and their grown children, and he noticed something curious: very tall parents had tall kids, but just a little closer to average. He called this "regressing toward the mean," and the line he drew through all those points gave us the word we still use today. The specific finding faded, but the method stuck around — fitting the best line through a cloud of points, no matter what the cloud is about. And today, our cloud is box height and distance.

concept-features-target.script: Let's start with the basic shape of every problem we'll tackle. On one side we have features, the things we already know, like how many hours you studied or the size of a house. On the other side is the target, the single number we want to predict, like a test score or a price. A model is really just a learned relationship between those inputs and that number, and regression's whole job is to find the line that captures that relationship best. What "best" actually means, we'll pin down in just a moment.

concept-loss.script: So how do we know when a line actually fits our data well? We measure our wrongness with something called loss, and here we're using Mean Squared Error, which squares every gap between our prediction and the truth. Squaring is clever because it makes negatives disappear and it punishes big misses far more than small ones. Look at the numbers: the too-flat and too-steep lines score around 52 or 53, while our best-fit line drops to about 5. Just remember, chasing loss all the way to zero can backfire — that's overfitting, and we'll dig into it next class.

quiz-loss.script: Alright, quick gut check before we move on. We've got two lines trying to fit the same scatter of points—one has an SSE of 12, the other 340. Which one does the data actually prefer? Remember, SSE measures total wrongness, so a smaller number means the predictions land closer to the real points. So Line A, with its tiny 12, is the winner—lower loss always means a better fit.

concept-gradient-descent.script: Imagine you're standing on a mountain, blindfolded, and you want to reach the valley floor. You can't see the whole landscape, but you can feel which way slopes downhill under your feet — so you take a small step that direction, then repeat, thousands of times. That's gradient descent: at each spot you find the steepest direction and step the opposite way, toward lower error. And that step size, the learning rate, really matters — too small and you crawl forever, too big and you overshoot the valley and bounce around. Today in Lab 1, you'll build this exact loop yourself in just a few lines of code.

concept-train-test.script: Here's an idea you've actually met before, and I love that. We split our data into two piles: one the model learns from, and one it never sees until judgment day. Why bother? Because if you test on the same rows the model trained on, you're just measuring memorization, not real learning. That's the overfitting trap we warned about — score on fresh data, and only then do you get an honest number.

case-av-regression.script: Here's a real example we'll keep coming back to. Imagine estimating how far away a car is just from the height of its bounding box in pixels: bigger box, closer car, roughly a straight line. Inside the range the model trained on, this works beautifully. But push it too far, and the line will happily tell you a car is negative six meters away, which is impossible. That absurd answer isn't a bug you'll create in the lab — it's the lesson, and it's exactly why we'll need non-linear models later.

discuss-linear-things.script: Let's take five minutes to hunt for straight lines in the real world. With a partner, name two things you think rise together in a roughly straight line — maybe hours studied and test scores, or height and shoe size — but pick something you could actually measure. Then stress-test it: would a straight line really fit all the way, or does it start to curve at the extremes? Trust me, most relationships bend somewhere, so find the spot where yours breaks and share it.

lab-gradient-descent.script: Okay, here's the moment where "training a model" stops being magic and becomes something you can actually read. We start with two numbers, m and b, both at zero — a terrible line — and we let this loop nudge them downhill, over and over, two thousand times. Watch the loss plummet from around five thousand down to almost nothing, and notice that the numbers we land on match the exact formula a mathematician would hand you. Then try the challenges: crank the learning rate up to point-oh-five and watch the whole thing explode, because we've stepped too far and overshot the valley.

reference-key-terms.script: Let me walk you through the words we'll lean on today. Your features are the inputs you know, and your target is what you're trying to predict—we call those X and y. Loss, measured here as mean squared error, tells us how wrong our predictions are on average, and gradient descent is how we shrink that loss, taking downhill steps whose size is set by the learning rate. R-squared tells us what fraction of the variation we've actually explained, where one is perfect and zero means we're no better than guessing the average. And keep an eye on extrapolation—predicting beyond your training data, where a line keeps answering even when it really shouldn't.

backup-multiple-regression.script: So some of you are already thinking, "Wait, why are we stuck with just one input?" Great question, and the answer is you're not. backup-regularization.script: Here's a question worth sitting with: what happens when a model tries too hard? When you've got lots of features, plain regression can hand enormous weights to noisy columns, basically memorizing quirks instead of learning the real trend — and that's just overfitting wearing a new costume. The fix is elegant: we add a penalty for large coefficients, so the model has to justify every big weight, giving us smaller, steadier numbers that generalize better. You don't need the math today, just remember the names Ridge and Lasso, and the shape of the idea — penalize complexity, not just error.
